terms.gloss: it’s getting light already, day is breaking
terms.grammar: impersonal inchoative of lūceō; comedy often adds a vague hoc as subject
terms.comment: What Plautus’s and Terence’s people say when the night is over, and Cicero in a letter written before dawn. The editions print lūciscit in Terence and Cicero, lūcēscit in Plautus; Lewis & Short gives both. For its opposite see “it’s getting dark”.

evidence: Plaut. Mil. 218: vigilā inquam, expergīscere inquam, lūcet hoc inquam.
Sen. Ep. 122.9: lūcet: somnī tempus est

terms.gloss: dawn is breaking (of the first grey light)
evidence: Liv. 36.24: jam dīlūcēscēbat, cum signum cōnsul dedit
terms.comment: The word of narrative prose, most often in a cum-clause.

phrases.english: It’s getting light already; the birds are starting to sing.
Is it light yet? — Not yet; go to sleep.
Let’s go, Amphitryon. It’s getting light now.

phrases.latin: Et jam lūcēscēbat omniaque sub oculīs erant.
phrases.english: And by now it was getting light, and everything was in plain view.

sources: Lewis & Short: lucesco · Lewis & Short: dilucesco · Lewis & Short: luceo
